concepts.explainer:
**What it is.** Under quantitative easing (QE) the central bank buys government bonds (and sometimes other bonds), paying for them with newly created bank reserves. Under quantitative tightening (QT) it does the opposite: it does not reinvest maturing bonds, or sells them actively, shrinking its balance sheet.

**Mechanism.** QE takes long-dated bonds out of the market: the extra demand pushes up their prices and lowers long-term yields, especially the term premium. Those who sold the bonds to the central bank reinvest in riskier assets (portfolio rebalancing): tighter spreads, more expensive equities. QT increases the bonds the private market has to absorb and tends to push up long-term yields and reduce liquidity.

**Winners and losers.** QE favours holders of financial assets and indebted governments, which borrow at lower cost. QT weighs on long maturities and on the weakest issuers.

**What to watch.** Pace of QT (billions per month), active sales or simply no reinvestment, the level of bank reserves, strains in repo rates.
concepts.interview: QE and QT let you show that monetary policy is not just the policy rate: the central bank also acts on the long end of the curve. Link it to the cost of long-dated debt and to market liquidity. EN: "Even with policy rates on hold, as long as QT continues private investors have to absorb more duration, which supports a higher term premium and long-end yields, and that matters for anyone pricing long-dated debt."
watch: Is the pace of QT changing: speeding up, slowing down or stopping?
Active sales, or only no reinvestment of maturing bonds?
Are bank reserves still ample? Are there strains in repo?
How are long-term yields reacting?

questions.stem: Through which main channel does quantitative easing (QE) lower long-term interest rates?
options: The central bank buys long-dated bonds in size, pushing prices up and yields down
The central bank cuts the overnight policy rate to zero and commits to keep it there
The central bank sells long-dated bonds to commercial banks, pushing their prices down
The central bank prints banknotes and sends them directly to every household to spend

steps: Under QE the central bank becomes a large buyer of long-dated bonds.
The extra demand pushes bond prices up; since price and yield move in opposite directions, long-term yields fall.
QE works mainly on the long end, whereas a cut in the policy rate works on the short end.
explanation.shortcut: QE = central bank buys bonds = prices up = long-term yields down.
explanation.trap: Confusing QE with a rate cut: they are different tools, often used when the policy rate is already close to zero.
explanation.rule: QE compresses long-term yields, in particular the term premium.

questions.stem: Under quantitative tightening (QT), a central bank lets maturing bonds roll off without reinvesting. What is the most likely effect on long-term yields, other things equal?
options: Upward pressure, because private investors must absorb more bond supply
Downward pressure, because fewer government bonds remain outstanding in the market
No effect, because QT only changes short-term money-market rates
Downward pressure, because bank reserves increase and banks buy more bonds

steps: When a bond held by the central bank matures, the government repays it and has to issue new debt to refinance it.
Without reinvestment, that new debt has to be bought by private investors rather than by the central bank.
More supply for the private market to absorb means lower prices and higher yields, especially at the long end.
explanation.shortcut: QT = the central bank stops buying = more supply for private investors = yields up.
explanation.trap: Thinking QT reduces the bonds outstanding: the government keeps issuing; only the buyer changes.
explanation.rule: QT acts like an increase in the net supply of duration to the market.

questions.stem: Why is QE said to work partly through "portfolio rebalancing"?
options: QE forces banks to rebalance their capital ratios by issuing new shares to outside investors
Governments must rebalance their budgets, by law, whenever the central bank buys their debt
Bond sellers reinvest the cash they receive in riskier assets, such as credit and equities
Investors shift from equities into cash, which lowers stock prices and market volatility

steps: Those who sell government bonds to the central bank end up holding cash that earns little.
To maintain their portfolio's return they buy similar but riskier assets: corporate bonds, high yield, equities.
The demand spreads across the whole market: tighter credit spreads, higher equity valuations, a lower cost of capital for companies.
explanation.shortcut: QE pushes investors out along the risk curve.
explanation.trap: Thinking QE affects only government bonds: the effect is transmitted to credit and equities.
explanation.rule: QE lowers yields on safe assets and pushes demand towards riskier assets.

pill.why: Central bank balance sheet policy usually works through long-term yields: QE lowers term premia and pushes investors into riskier assets, while QT tends to do the opposite.
pill.watch: The pace of QT, active sales versus run-off, and signs of strain in repo markets.
pill.en: [Central bank] is [slowing/speeding up] [QT/QE], which matters for long-term yields because private investors will need to absorb [more/less] government debt.

concepts.title: Credit spreads and defaults
concepts.explainer:
**What it is.** The credit spread is the extra yield a company pays over a government bond of the same maturity: it compensates for default risk and lower liquidity. The market splits into investment grade (rated BBB- and above) and high yield (below BBB-, also called "junk").

**Mechanism.** When the outlook worsens, investors demand more spread: the cost of debt rises, refinancing becomes difficult and defaults increase, especially among highly leveraged companies with near-term maturities (the maturity wall). A downgrade from BBB- to BB+ (a "fallen angel") takes the issuer into high yield and forces many funds to sell, because they can hold only investment grade.

**Winners and losers.** Tight spreads favour issuers, LBOs and leveraged finance. Wide spreads hurt indebted companies and their sponsors, but open up opportunities for distressed debt and private credit funds, as well as for restructuring teams.

**What to watch.** IG and HY spread indices, default rates, CDS, debt maturing in the next 2 years, net debt/EBITDA and interest cover.
concepts.interview: Credit is central to DCM, leveraged finance and restructuring: show that you can connect spreads, refinancing and defaults. Mentioning the growth of private credit as an alternative to the bond market is a good sign of sector awareness. EN: "Spreads have widened, so borrowers facing a maturity wall may struggle to refinance in the public market, which is exactly where private credit funds and restructuring advisers come in."
watch: Are IG and HY spreads widening or tightening?
Is the default rate rising, and in which sectors?
How much debt matures in the next 12-24 months?
The issuer's leverage (net debt/EBITDA) and interest cover.

questions.stem: A corporate bond yields 6.2% and a government bond with the same maturity yields 4.0%. What is the credit spread?
options: 22 bps
220 bps
155 bps

steps: Credit spread = corporate yield - government yield of the same maturity.
explanation.shortcut: Difference in percentage points × 100 = bps.
explanation.trap: Taking the ratio 6.2 / 4.0 = 1.55 instead of the difference, or getting the conversion into bps wrong.
explanation.rule: The spread is a difference between yields, expressed in bps.

questions.stem: A company's credit rating is cut from BBB- to BB+. Why can its bond prices fall sharply on this particular downgrade?
options: BB+ is a default rating, so bondholders immediately stop receiving their coupon payments
It drops from investment grade to high yield, so investment-grade-only funds must sell
Coupons are automatically cut by the issuer after any one-notch downgrade of its rating
The bonds must be repaid early, at a discount, whenever the issuer's rating is cut

steps: BBB- is the lowest notch of investment grade; BB+ is the highest notch of high yield.
Many investors (IG funds, insurers, some pension funds) can hold only investment grade, by mandate or by regulation.
The change of category triggers forced selling by holders who can no longer keep the bond: the price falls more than a single rating notch would justify.
explanation.shortcut: BBB- → BB+ = fallen angel = forced selling.
explanation.trap: Thinking high yield means default: BB+ is still an issuer that pays, just a riskier one.
explanation.rule: The IG/HY boundary matters more than any other rating notch because of investor constraints.

questions.stem: A company has 500m of floating-rate debt and EBITDA of 100m. Its all-in interest rate rises from 6% to 9%, as base rates increase and the debt is refinanced at a wider credit spread. What happens to its interest cover (EBITDA / interest expense)?
options: It falls from 5.0x to about 3.3x
It falls from about 3.3x to about 2.2x
It falls from about 3.3x to about 3.0x
It is unchanged, because EBITDA is unchanged

steps: Interest before: 500m × 6% = 30m. Cover = 100 / 30 = 3.3x.
Interest after: 500m × 9% = 45m. Cover = 100 / 45 = 2.2x.
With the same leverage (5.0x debt/EBITDA), the capacity to service the debt falls by a third: this is how a rise in rates and spreads drives defaults up.
explanation.shortcut: Cover = EBITDA / (debt × rate): if the rate rises by 50%, cover falls by a third.
explanation.trap: Confusing leverage (debt/EBITDA = 5.0x, which does not change) with interest cover.
explanation.rule: Leverage and interest cover measure different things: the latter is sensitive to rates.

pill.why: Credit spreads usually price default risk and set corporate funding costs: when they widen, refinancing gets harder, especially for leveraged issuers facing near-term maturities.
pill.watch: IG and HY spread indices, default rates by sector and the upcoming maturity wall.
pill.en: Credit spreads in [market] have [widened/tightened] by [X bps], which [raises/lowers] refinancing costs for leveraged borrowers in [sector] and [slows/supports] LBO financing.

concepts.title: Equity markets
concepts.explainer:
**What it is.** News on equity indices (S&P 500, Nasdaq, FTSE 100, Euro Stoxx 50, DAX, Nikkei) and on big market moves: rallies, sell-offs, corrections (a fall of 10% from the highs) and bear markets (a fall of 20%).

**Mechanism.** The level of an index depends on expected earnings and on how much the market is willing to pay for them, i.e. the multiple (for example the P/E). The multiple moves with rates and risk appetite: falling real rates and positive sentiment expand it. Many indices are weighted by market capitalisation, so a few large stocks can drive the whole index: check the breadth, i.e. how many stocks take part in the move.

**Winners and losers.** Sectors rotate: with falling rates, growth stocks and small caps win; with strong growth, cyclicals; in a slowdown, defensives. A strong market opens the window for IPOs and equity raises; a sell-off shuts it.

**What to watch.** Is the move driven by earnings or by multiples? Which sectors are leading? Index concentration, volatility, flows.
concepts.interview: When you discuss a market move, break it down: earnings or multiples, which sectors, which macro cause. Then link it to the bank's business: high valuations and low volatility favour IPOs and acquisitions paid in shares. EN: "The rally has been driven more by multiple expansion than by earnings upgrades, and it is concentrated in a handful of large caps, so I would watch market breadth before calling a sustained reopening of the IPO window."
watch: Is the move driven by earnings or by multiples?
How many stocks are taking part (breadth) and which sectors are leading?
What are rates and volatility doing at the same time?
Is the window for IPOs and equity raises open?

questions.stem: An equity index falls from a peak of 5,000 to 4,000. How is this move usually described?
options: A correction, since the index has lost 25% from its peak
A correction, since the index is down 10% from its peak
A bull market, since volatility has risen
A bear market, since the index is down 20% from its peak

steps: Market convention: correction = a fall of at least 10% from the highs; bear market = a fall of at least 20%.
At -20% the index has entered a bear market.
explanation.shortcut: -10% correction, -20% bear market, always measured from the peak.
explanation.trap: Dividing by the final value (1,000 / 4,000 = 25%): the correct base is the starting peak.
explanation.rule: Moves from the highs are calculated on the starting value.

questions.stem: An index trades on a P/E of 20x. Expected earnings rise 5% while the P/E multiple falls to 19x. Approximately what happens to the index level?
options: About +5%, in line with the earnings growth
About -5%, in line with the lower multiple
About -0.25%: the index is roughly unchanged
About +10%, since both effects push the same way

steps: Price = P/E × earnings.
The index falls by about 0.25%: earnings growth (+5%) is almost entirely offset by the contraction in the multiple (-5%).
explanation.shortcut: % change in price ≈ % change in earnings + % change in the multiple.
explanation.trap: Looking only at earnings (+5%) and ignoring the de-rating of the multiple.
explanation.rule: Every market move can be broken down into earnings and multiple.

questions.stem: A market-capitalisation-weighted index rises 2% on a day when most of its constituents fall. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The index must be equally weighted, so the average constituent must in fact have risen
Constituents that fall on the day are temporarily excluded from the index calculation
Dividends paid by the falling constituents are added back to the index level that day
A few mega-cap stocks rose sharply and dominate the index weights, so breadth was weak

steps: In a cap-weighted index each stock is weighted in proportion to its market capitalisation.
If a few very large stocks rise sharply, they can push the index up even if most stocks fall.
Breadth (the ratio of advancing to declining stocks) reveals this: narrow, concentrated rallies are considered more fragile.
explanation.shortcut: Index up with most stocks down = rally driven by a few large caps.
explanation.trap: Thinking the index represents the average stock: for that you need an equal-weighted index.
explanation.rule: In cap-weighted indices, always check concentration and breadth.

pill.why: Index moves usually reflect either earnings expectations or the multiple investors will pay, and strong markets tend to open the window for IPOs and capital raises.
pill.watch: Whether earnings or multiples drive the move, market breadth and which sectors lead.
pill.en: The [index] moved [X%], led by [sector]; the driver looks like [earnings/multiples], and [narrow/broad] breadth suggests the move is [fragile/durable].

concepts.title: Mergers and acquisitions (M&A)

\b(?:health services?|health trusts?|care trusts?|ambulance services?|fire services?|police services?)\b.{0,40}\bmerg\w*|\bmerg\w*\b.{0,40}\b(?:health services?|health trusts?)\b|\bdark money\b|^op[- ]?ed\b
concepts.explainer:
An **acquisition** is the purchase of control of another company; a **merger** combines two companies into one. The acquirer usually pays a **premium** to the market price (typically 20-40%) to persuade the target's shareholders to sell: this is why the target's shares rise on the announcement, while the acquirer's often fall if the market fears it is overpaying.

The premium is justified mainly by **synergies**: cost synergies (closing duplicate sites, purchasing at greater scale) or revenue synergies (cross-selling), which are easier to promise than to deliver.

The **form of payment** also matters: in **cash** (funded from cash on hand or debt) the acquirer keeps all the upside and all the risk; in **shares** the target's shareholders become shareholders in the acquirer, the risk is shared, but the existing shareholders are diluted.

What to watch: the premium paid, the EV/EBITDA multiple, the announced synergies, the **accretion/dilution** effect on EPS and the reaction of the acquirer's shares.
concepts.interview:
In an interview, do not just say that a deal has happened: explain the strategic logic (scale, new geographies, technology), how it was paid for and whether the premium is justified by the synergies. Close with a concrete risk, such as integration or antitrust.

EN: I found this deal interesting because the buyer is paying roughly a [X]% premium, which only makes sense if it delivers the [cost/revenue] synergies it has announced, and the reaction in the acquirer's shares suggests investors are [sceptical/supportive].
watch: How large is the premium relative to the undisturbed price, before the rumours?
Payment in cash, in shares or mixed, and with how much new debt?
Are the synergies cost synergies (more credible) or revenue synergies?
How do the acquirer's shares react on the day of the announcement?

questions.stem: In a typical public takeover, how do the share prices of the target and the acquirer usually react on the announcement day?
options: Both rise by a similar amount, because the synergies benefit all shareholders
The target rises towards the offer price, while the acquirer is flat or falls
The target falls because it loses its independence, while the acquirer rises
Neither moves until completion, because the outcome is uncertain before closing

steps: The acquirer offers a premium to the target's market price, so the target's shares rise towards the offer price.
They usually stay slightly below the offer (the merger arbitrage spread), because the deal could fall through, for example on antitrust grounds, and payment arrives only at closing.
The acquirer is the one paying that premium: if the market thinks the synergies do not cover it, its shares stay flat or fall.
explanation.shortcut: Whoever receives the premium rises; whoever pays it suffers.
explanation.trap: Thinking that synergies lift both share prices: much of their value is passed on to the target's shareholders through the premium.
explanation.rule: On announcement, value shifts from the acquirer to the target through the premium.

questions.stem: An acquirer's management believes its own shares are significantly undervalued by the market. Other things equal, which form of payment is it most likely to prefer for an acquisition?
options: All-stock, because issuing shares avoids taking on new debt
All-stock, because target shareholders always prefer to receive shares
It makes no difference, because the headline deal value is the same either way
Cash, because paying with undervalued shares would give away too much of the company

steps: Paying in shares means issuing new shares to the target's shareholders.
If your shares are undervalued, you have to issue more of them to pay the same price: you are giving value away to the new shareholders.
With cash, by contrast, the existing shareholders keep all the upside when the market re-rates the shares upwards.

Conversely, a company that considers its own shares expensive prefers to pay in shares: this is why the market often reads an all-stock deal as a signal that management considers its own shares expensive, or at least not trading at a discount.
explanation.shortcut: Undervalued shares: pay cash. Overvalued shares: pay in shares.
explanation.trap: Thinking that the form of payment is neutral: the headline value of the deal is the same, but it changes who bears the risk and who captures the upside.
explanation.rule: The form of payment signals what management thinks of the value of its own shares.

questions.stem: In an all-stock deal, the acquirer trades on a P/E of 20x and buys the target at a P/E of 25x (offer price divided by the target's EPS). Ignoring synergies and deal costs, what is the effect on the acquirer's EPS?
options: Accretive, because the combined company earns more in total
Neutral, because no cash leaves the company in an all-stock deal
Dilutive, because the acquirer pays a higher P/E than its own
Accretive, because the target is valued on a higher multiple

steps: Rule: in an all-stock deal, compare the P/Es. If the P/E paid for the target is higher than the acquirer's P/E, the deal is dilutive.
Example: an acquirer with earnings of 100, 100 shares, EPS of 1.00 and a share price of 20 (P/E 20x). It pays 25 times the target's earnings of 40, i.e. 1,000.
It issues 1,000 / 20 = 50 new shares. New EPS = (100 + 40) / 150 = 0.93, below 1.00: dilutive.
Synergies could offset this, but the question excludes them.
explanation.shortcut: All-stock: P/E paid higher than the acquirer's P/E = dilutive; lower = accretive.
explanation.trap: Thinking that higher total earnings mean higher EPS: what counts is earnings per share, and the newly issued shares dilute it.
explanation.rule: In a share-for-share deal, there is accretion only if the acquirer's P/E exceeds the P/E paid for the target.

pill.why: M&A announcements usually lift the target's shares towards the offer price, while the buyer's reaction shows whether investors think the synergies justify the premium.
pill.watch: The premium to the undisturbed price, the cash/share mix, synergy type and EPS accretion or dilution.
pill.en: [Acquirer] is offering a [X%] premium for [target], about [X]x EBITDA, which only makes sense if [cost/revenue] synergies of [amount] are actually delivered.

concepts.title: Hostile bids and activism
concepts.explainer:
A **hostile bid** is a takeover attempt that the target's board rejects: the bidder then goes directly to shareholders, with a public offer (tender offer) or by trying to replace the board through a **proxy fight**. The offer is often raised (sweetened bid) and a rival may emerge: this opens a **bidding war**, excellent for the target's shareholders and risky for whoever wins by overpaying (winner's curse).

An **activist investor** buys a minority stake in a company it considers undervalued and demands changes: buybacks, disposals of divisions, cost cuts, new directors or the sale of the whole company. The shares usually rise when the stake becomes public.

The board can defend itself with a **poison pill** (in the US) or by seeking a **white knight**, a friendly buyer. In the UK the Takeover Code limits defences and gives the bidder 28 days to make a firm offer or walk away (put up or shut up).

What to watch: how much the offer is raised, who owns the shares and what the activist is asking for.
concepts.interview:
A hostile battle or an activist campaign is an excellent talking point because it shows the conflict between the board and shareholders over the value of the company. Explain what each side argues and which argument seems more credible to you in terms of value.

EN: What I find interesting is that the board says the offer undervalues the company while the bidder argues it is a full price, so the real question for shareholders is whether management's standalone plan can credibly deliver more than [X] per share.
watch: Is the board rejecting the offer because it is too low or for strategic reasons?
Is the target trading above the offer price? Then the market expects a higher offer.
What stake does the activist hold and what exactly is it asking for?
Are there regulatory deadlines, such as the 28 days under the UK Takeover Code?

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a hostile takeover bid and a friendly one?
options: A hostile bid lacks the target board's support, so the bidder goes directly to shareholders
A hostile bid is always paid in cash, while a friendly bid is always paid in shares
A hostile bid is illegal in most European countries, so it can only happen in the US
A hostile bid always offers a lower premium than a friendly bid for the same company

steps: Whether a bid is friendly or hostile depends on the position of the target's board, not on the price or the form of payment.
If the board recommends the offer to shareholders, it is friendly; if the board rejects it and the bidder persists, it is hostile.
The hostile bidder bypasses the board: a direct offer to shareholders or a proxy fight to replace the directors.
explanation.shortcut: Ask yourself: does the board recommend the offer? If not, it is hostile.
explanation.trap: Believing that hostile means illegal or at a discount: on the contrary, a hostile bid often has to pay a higher premium to win over shareholders.
explanation.rule: Hostile = without the board's support, addressed directly to shareholders.

questions.stem: After a cash takeover offer is announced, the target's shares trade consistently above the offer price. What is the market most likely signalling?
options: The deal is likely to be blocked by competition regulators
The bidder is likely to withdraw its offer in the coming weeks
Investors expect a higher offer from the bidder or a rival bid
The acquirer's own shares are overvalued by the market

steps: Normally the target trades slightly below the offer price: the discount compensates for the risk of the deal falling through and for the time until payment.
If it trades above, investors are paying more than the current offer: they do so only if they expect to receive more.
So the market is pricing in a higher offer from the bidder or the arrival of a competing bidder (bidding war).
explanation.shortcut: Below the offer = deal risk; above the offer = expected higher bid.
explanation.trap: Thinking of antitrust risk: fear of a block would push the shares below the offer, not above it.
explanation.rule: The spread between the market price and the offer tells you what the market expects about the outcome of the deal.

questions.stem: An activist investor buys a stake in a conglomerate that trades at a discount to the sum of its parts. Which demand is most consistent with closing that discount?
options: Raising new debt to fund a large acquisition in an unrelated sector
Adding more businesses to the group to diversify its sources of earnings
Cutting the dividend to build up a larger cash reserve for future acquisitions
Separating or selling divisions so each is valued on its own peers' multiple

steps: Conglomerate discount: the market values the group at less than the sum of the values of its divisions taken on their own (sum of the parts).
Example: two divisions would be worth 6 and 4 billion on their own (10 in total), but the group's market capitalisation is 8: a 20% discount.
By separating or selling the divisions, each one is priced on its own peers' multiple and the discount closes.
Diversifying further or building up cash tends to widen the discount, not reduce it.
explanation.shortcut: Discount to the sum of the parts: the typical solution is to separate the parts.
explanation.trap: Thinking that diversification is rewarded: investors can diversify on their own, so they rarely pay a premium for a conglomerate.
explanation.rule: Activists create value by closing the gap between price and value: buybacks, disposals, spin-offs, governance.

pill.why: Hostile bids and activist stakes usually put a company 'in play': the target's shares tend to rise on expectations of a higher offer, rival bidder or break-up.
pill.watch: Whether the board rejects on price or strategy, and whether the shares trade above the offer.
pill.en: [Bidder/activist] is pressing [company] for [a sale/break-up/buyback]; the share price reaction shows how much of [a higher bid/value release] the market already expects.

concepts.title: Antitrust and merger control
match: ^(?!.*\b(migration|migrants?|asylum|rule of law|hungary|poland|member states?|privacy|data protection|gdpr|digital services act|dsa|emissions|fishing)\b).*\b(eu|brussels|european commission)\b.{0,30}\b(fines?|fined)\b
concepts.explainer:
**Antitrust** authorities (the European Commission, the CMA in the UK, the FTC and DOJ in the US) police two things: **mergers** that reduce competition and the conduct of dominant companies (abuse of a dominant position, price-fixing cartels).

The mechanism: if two competitors merge and their combined share is high, the new company could raise prices or innovate less. The authority can approve the deal, approve it with **remedies** (selling part of the business, behavioural commitments) or block it, often after an in-depth investigation (Phase 2) that lasts months.

Who loses: the target if the deal falls through (its shares fall back towards the pre-offer price) and the acquirer, which may have to pay a **reverse break fee** or sell assets. Who gains: competitors and, in theory, customers. In the EU, fines for abuse can reach 10% of global turnover.

What to watch: the overlap between the businesses, market shares, the timing of the review and the remedies proposed.
concepts.interview:
Linking a deal to antitrust risk shows maturity: bankers assess the probability of approval and the possible remedies as early as when they structure the transaction. You can say whether the deal is horizontal (direct competitors, high risk) or vertical (supplier and customer, lower risk).

EN: The strategic logic is clear, but given the combined market share in [segment] I would expect a lengthy review and possibly divestments as a remedy, which is why the target still trades at a discount to the offer price.
watch: Is the deal horizontal (direct competitors) or vertical?
Combined market shares and the number of competitors that remain
Is the spread between the target's price and the offer widening or narrowing?
Are remedies or a reverse break fee provided for?

questions.stem: Which type of merger is most likely to face intense scrutiny from competition authorities?
options: A merger between a component supplier and one of its many small customers
A merger between two large companies operating in completely unrelated industries
A merger between two direct competitors with a large combined market share
A merger between two small firms in a highly fragmented market with many rivals

steps: Antitrust review looks at how much competition is reduced after the deal.
A horizontal merger between large direct competitors eliminates a rival and raises the combined share: a risk of higher prices for customers.
Vertical mergers or mergers across unrelated sectors rarely eliminate a direct competitor; in a fragmented market, two small players do not change the market structure.
explanation.shortcut: Horizontal + high share = maximum antitrust scrutiny.
explanation.trap: Thinking that the absolute size of the companies is what counts: what counts is the overlap in the same market.
explanation.rule: Antitrust risk grows with the overlap between the businesses and with market concentration.

questions.stem: A cash offer of 50 per share is made for a target whose undisturbed share price was 35. Because of antitrust uncertainty, the target trades at 45. Ignoring time value, and assuming the price falls back to 35 if the deal is blocked, what probability of completion is the market implying?
options: About 33%
About 67%
About 78%
About 90%

steps: The market price is a weighted average of the two outcomes: p x 50 + (1 - p) x 35 = 45.
Simplify: 35 + 15p = 45, so 15p = 10.
explanation.shortcut: p = (current price - price without the deal) / (offer - price without the deal) = 10 / 15.
explanation.trap: Calculating 45 / 50 = 90%: this ignores that if the deal falls through the shares do not go to zero, but fall back to 35.
explanation.rule: Implied probability = (price - downside) / (offer - downside).

questions.stem: To win clearance for a horizontal merger, the acquirer agrees to sell the business where the two firms overlap. What is this, and what is its typical effect on the deal for the acquirer?
options: A structural remedy: it eases approval but usually reduces the deal's synergies
A behavioural remedy: it has no effect on the deal's value because only conduct changes
A break fee: it compensates the target's shareholders if the deal fails to complete
A structural remedy: it always increases the deal's value because the sale raises cash

steps: Selling a business is a structural remedy: it removes the overlap that concerns the authority.
A behavioural remedy, by contrast, is a commitment on future conduct (prices, access, licences), which European authorities regard as less reliable.
The disposal secures approval, but the overlap was often the main source of the cost synergies: the deal is worth less to the acquirer.
In addition, the business has to be sold by a deadline, and therefore often at an unfavourable price.
explanation.shortcut: Asset disposal = structural remedy; the cost is the lost synergies.
explanation.trap: Thinking that the sale proceeds always increase value: you are selling under pressure and losing part of the deal's logic.
explanation.rule: Remedies buy approval, but the price is paid in synergies.

pill.why: Competition reviews often decide whether and when big deals close, and remedies, blocks or fines can materially change a company's value and strategy.
pill.watch: Combined market shares, whether a Phase 2 probe opens, proposed remedies and the target's deal spread.
pill.en: The [authority] review is the key risk for [deal]: a combined [X%] share of [market] makes [remedies/a Phase 2 probe] likely, and the deal spread reflects it.

concepts.title: Private equity and LBOs
concepts.explainer:
A **private equity** fund buys companies, sometimes taking them off the stock market through a **take-private**, and finances the purchase with a lot of **debt**, often 40-60% of the price: this is the **leveraged buyout** (LBO). The debt sits on the acquired company and is repaid from its cash flows.

The fund's return (IRR, multiple on invested capital or MOIC) comes from three levers: EBITDA growth, **debt reduction** using free cash flow and **multiple expansion**, i.e. selling at a higher multiple than the purchase multiple. Leverage amplifies returns on equity, but also losses.

This is why interest rates matter so much: high rates make debt expensive, lower the price the fund can pay and slow deals down; falling rates revive them. Funds also have a lot of **dry powder** (capital raised but not yet invested), which pushes them to buy.

What to watch: the multiple paid, leverage (debt / EBITDA), who is lending (banks or **private credit**) and how the fund plans to exit: IPO, sale to a strategic buyer or sale to another fund.
concepts.interview:
Private equity news is perfect for showing that you understand the logic of an LBO. Explain why that business is a good candidate (stable cash, low capex, margins with room for improvement) and how interest rates affect the price the fund can pay.

EN: This looks like a classic LBO candidate, with stable cash flows, low capital intensity and room for operational improvement; with financing costs still [high/falling], returns will depend more on deleveraging and EBITDA growth than on multiple expansion.
watch: Does the business generate stable, predictable cash?
Leverage: how many times EBITDA is the debt?
Is the premium paid to public shareholders high or low?
How and when will the fund be able to exit?

questions.stem: Which characteristic makes a company most attractive as a leveraged buyout target?
options: High revenue growth funded by negative free cash flow
A large share of revenue from a single, volatile project
A high existing debt load and few tangible assets
Stable, predictable cash flows and low capital expenditure

steps: In an LBO the company has to repay a large amount of debt from its own cash.
So it needs stable, predictable cash flows, and little capex to absorb them.
A fast-growing company with negative free cash flow would be unable to pay the interest and the debt repayments.
explanation.shortcut: LBO = cash machine: look for stable free cash flow, not growth at any cost.
explanation.trap: Choosing the highest growth: without cash to service the debt, leverage turns into default risk.
explanation.rule: The ideal LBO candidate has stable cash, low capex, little existing debt and margins with room for improvement.

questions.stem: A fund buys a company for 1,000 (400 of equity and 600 of debt) and sells it five years later, still for an enterprise value of 1,000, after using cash flow to repay 300 of the debt. Ignoring fees, what multiple of money (MOIC) does the fund earn on its equity?

steps: At exit the enterprise value is still 1,000, but the debt has fallen from 600 to 300.
Equity at exit = 1,000 - 300 = 700.
MOIC = 700 / 400 = 1.75x: the entire gain comes from paying down debt (deleveraging).
explanation.shortcut: Exit equity = exit EV - remaining debt; then divide by the equity invested.
explanation.trap: Thinking that without any growth in value the fund ends up at 1.0x: repaying debt with cash shifts value from the lenders to the equity.
explanation.rule: The three levers of an LBO: EBITDA growth, deleveraging, multiple expansion.

questions.stem: Other things equal, how does a sharp rise in interest rates typically affect leveraged buyout activity?
options: It lowers the price a fund can pay for the same target return, so deal activity tends to fall
It raises the price a fund can pay, because lenders are keener to lend at higher rates
It has no real effect, because the fund can simply replace the debt with equity without lowering its returns
It increases deal activity, because sellers rush to sell before valuations fall

steps: With higher rates every euro of debt costs more: with the same cash, the company can support less debt.
Less debt means more equity for the same price, and therefore a lower IRR for the same price paid.
To keep its target IRR the fund has to offer less; sellers often do not accept, and deal volumes fall.
In addition, high rates tend to compress the multiples at which the fund will be able to sell.
explanation.shortcut: Rates up = sustainable debt down = affordable price down.
explanation.trap: Thinking the fund can replace debt with equity without consequences: with less leverage the IRR on equity falls, so to stay on its target return it has to offer less.
explanation.rule: The cost of debt is a key input into the price a private equity fund can pay.

pill.why: Buyouts are funded largely with debt, so private equity activity usually tracks financing conditions: cheaper debt and tighter spreads raise what sponsors can pay.
pill.watch: The entry multiple, leverage as a multiple of EBITDA, who lends, and the exit route.
pill.en: [Sponsor] is buying [target] at about [X]x EBITDA with [X]x leverage from [banks/private credit]; returns will depend on EBITDA growth, debt paydown and the exit multiple.

concepts.title: IPOs and stock market listings
concepts.explainer:
In an **IPO** (initial public offering) a company sells shares to the public for the first time and lists on the stock exchange. The shares can be **primary** (new: the money goes to the company to fund growth or reduce debt) or **secondary** (sold by existing shareholders, for example a private equity fund that is exiting).

The banks (bookrunners) collect orders from institutional investors during **bookbuilding** and, together with the company, set the price, usually at a small discount to ensure a good debut. A strong rise on the first day (**pop**) pleases the new investors, but means that the sellers left money on the table (underpricing).

IPOs are cyclical: the window opens when stock markets are rising and volatility is low, and closes at times of stress. This is why a recovery in IPOs is a sign of confidence.

What to watch: valuation relative to listed peers, the primary or secondary share of the offering, the price relative to the indicative range, performance at **lock-up** expiry and the choice of venue (London, New York, Amsterdam).
concepts.interview:
An IPO lets you talk about valuation, market conditions and the choice of listing venue, a hot topic in London. Explain why the company is listing now and what the price set relative to the range tells you.

EN: The IPO priced at the [top/bottom] of its range and [rose/fell] on its debut, which tells me investor appetite for [sector] is [strong/weak]; I would also watch the lock-up expiry, when existing holders are free to sell.
watch: Was the price set at the top, in the middle or below the indicative range?
How much of the proceeds goes to the company and how much to the selling shareholders?
Valuation relative to peers that are already listed
Performance in the first few weeks and at lock-up expiry

questions.stem: In an IPO, what is the key difference between primary and secondary shares?
options: Primary shares are sold by existing shareholders, while secondary shares are newly issued
Primary shares raise new money for the company; secondary shares are sold by existing holders
Primary shares are listed on the home exchange, while secondary shares are listed abroad
Primary shares carry voting rights, while secondary shares never do

steps: Primary shares are new shares issued by the company: the proceeds go to the company.
Secondary shares already exist and are sold by current shareholders (founders, private equity funds): the proceeds go to them.
This is why an IPO that is almost entirely secondary is read as an exit by shareholders, not as funding for growth.
explanation.shortcut: Primary = money to the company; secondary = money to the sellers.
explanation.trap: Confusing secondary shares with a listing on another exchange (secondary listing): it is a different concept.
explanation.rule: Always ask yourself who receives the IPO proceeds.

questions.stem: A company prices its IPO at 20 per share and the shares close their first day of trading at 26. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The company raised more money than if it had priced the IPO at 26
The company's enterprise value fell during the first day of trading
The bookrunners lost money because they had to buy back the shares
The IPO was underpriced, so the sellers left money on the table

steps: The company (and the selling shareholders) receive the IPO price, i.e. 20, not the first-day closing price.
If the market is immediately willing to pay 26, the demand was there at a higher price too.
The difference (6 per share, +30%) is value left to the IPO investors: underpricing.
A small pop is intended to reward buyers; a very large one points to overly cautious pricing.
explanation.shortcut: The first-day pop is a gift to IPO buyers, paid for by the sellers.
explanation.trap: Thinking that a big first-day rise brings more money to the company: the money has already been raised at the IPO price.
explanation.rule: Large pop = underpricing = money left on the table by the sellers.

questions.stem: Several large companies postpone their planned IPOs in the same month. Which market condition most likely explains this?
options: A rise in equity market volatility and falling valuations of listed peers
A fall in equity market volatility together with rising stock indices
A strong rally in the shares of companies that listed in recent months
Lower interest rates, which reduce companies' cost of equity capital

steps: IPOs need a market window: low volatility, rising indices, good performance by recent IPOs.
If volatility rises and listed peers lose value, investors demand bigger discounts and the achievable valuation falls.
Sellers prefer to postpone rather than list at a low price.
explanation.shortcut: Postponed IPOs = window closed = high volatility or falling valuations.
explanation.trap: Choosing lower interest rates: a lower cost of capital raises valuations and usually opens the window rather than closing it.
explanation.rule: IPO activity follows equity market confidence: it moves with the indices and with volatility.

pill.why: IPO activity usually signals market confidence: windows tend to open when equities rise and volatility is low, and pricing shows how much investors will pay for growth.
pill.watch: Pricing against the indicative range, primary versus secondary shares, and trading after lock-up expiry.
pill.en: [Company] priced its IPO at the [top/middle/bottom] of the range and [rose/fell] [X%] on debut, a useful read on whether the [market] listing window is really open.

concepts.title: Quarterly results and guidance
exclude: \b(fed|federal reserve|ecb|bank of england|boe|boj|bank of japan|bundesbank|banque de france|bank of italy|bank of canada|reserve bank|rba|snb|riksbank|norges bank|pboc|central bank|opec|iea|eia|moody['’]?s|fitch|s&p|rating agency|ratings agency)\b.{0,40}\b(outlook|forecasts?|guidance)\b
concepts.explainer:
Listed companies publish their **results** every quarter or half-year: revenue, margins, profit and **EPS**. The share price, however, does not react to the number itself but to the **surprise** relative to **consensus**, that is, the average of analysts' estimates. Profit growth of 10% can push the shares down if the market was expecting 15%.

Often **guidance**, management's indications about the future, matters even more: an upward revision to full-year forecasts moves the shares more than a good quarter, because the value of a share depends on future cash flows. A **profit warning** (in the UK often contained in a trading update) can trigger double-digit falls.

Also look at the **quality** of the result: revenue growth or just cost cuts? Organic growth or growth driven by acquisitions and currency effects? Margins expanding or shrinking? One-off items?

What to watch: a beat or miss on revenue and EPS, guidance raised or cut, comments on demand, prices and costs, the reaction of competitors.
concepts.interview:
When you mention a company's results, do not stop at 'profits went up': explain relative to what (consensus, guidance) and what drove the result. It is the simplest way to show that you think like an analyst.

EN: Although revenue grew [X]%, the shares fell because full-year guidance came in below consensus, which shows the market had been pricing in more than the company now expects.
watch: Does the result beat or miss consensus, and on which line (revenue, margins, EPS)?
Has full-year guidance been raised, confirmed or cut?
Does the beat come from demand or from cost cuts and one-off items?
What does management say about prices, volumes and costs?

questions.stem: A company reports earnings per share 10% higher than a year ago, but below the analysts' consensus estimate. What is the most likely immediate share price reaction?
options: A rise, because earnings grew by 10% year on year
No reaction, because past growth is already public information
A fall, because the result missed what the market had priced in
A rise, because consensus estimates are usually too optimistic anyway

steps: A share price already reflects the market's expectations, summarised in the consensus.
What matters is the surprise: actual result minus expected result.
Growth of 10% but below consensus = negative surprise: the shares tend to fall.
explanation.shortcut: The market compares the figure with expectations, not with last year.
explanation.trap: Stopping at the year-on-year growth: it is already in the price if the market expected it, and here it expected more.
explanation.rule: The price moves on the surprise relative to consensus.

questions.stem: A company beats consensus for the current quarter but cuts its full-year guidance. Why does the share price often fall?
options: Because any beat always triggers heavy profit-taking by short-term traders
Because lower expected future earnings outweigh one good quarter
Because beating consensus means the company will pay more tax next year
Because guidance matters mainly to bondholders, not to the company's shareholders

steps: The value of a share is the present value of all future cash flows, not of a single quarter.
A better quarter adds a small amount, and only once.
Lower guidance reduces profit estimates for the year and, usually, also for the following years on which the valuation is based.
Analysts cut their estimates, and the same multiple applied to lower earnings gives a lower price.
explanation.shortcut: Guidance carries more weight than the quarter: the future matters more than the past.
explanation.trap: Thinking the quarterly beat dominates: it is a figure about the past, while guidance speaks about the future.
explanation.rule: In results season, the direction of future estimates matters more than the historical figure.

questions.stem: A company beats EPS consensus, but revenue misses expectations and the EPS beat comes mainly from a lower tax rate and a one-off gain. How should an analyst judge the quality of the beat?
options: High quality, because EPS is the only figure that really drives the share price
High quality, because a lower tax rate is always a permanent improvement
Neutral, because revenue has no effect on valuation as long as EPS is higher
Low quality, because it does not come from sustainable operating performance

steps: A beat is high quality if it comes from revenue and operating margins, that is, from the part of the business that will recur.
A lower tax rate and a one-off gain will not recur: analysts strip them out of 'core' profit.
On top of that, revenue is below expectations: a sign of weak demand.
The market looks beyond EPS and often reacts badly.
explanation.shortcut: Ask yourself where the beat comes from: recurring revenue and operating margins are high quality; the tax rate, financial charges and one-off items are not.
explanation.trap: Stopping at the EPS number: a beat that stems from tax and exceptional items does not improve the outlook.
explanation.rule: Quality of earnings: revenue and operating margins matter more than tax and exceptional items.

pill.why: Share prices usually react to results versus consensus and to changes in guidance, because a company's value depends on future cash flows, not the last quarter.
pill.watch: Beat or miss on revenue and EPS, the guidance change and the quality of the beat.
pill.en: [Company] [beat/missed] consensus on [revenue/EPS] and [raised/cut] full-year guidance; the share reaction suggests the market cares more about [demand/margins] than the quarter itself.

concepts.title: Buybacks and dividends
match: \b(return|returns|returning|returned|hand back|hands back|handing back|handed back|give back|gives back)\b (up to )?(about |around |nearly )?((\$|£|€|us\$)\s?\d[\d.,]*\s?(bn|billion|m|mn|million)|cash|capital|surplus capital|excess capital|surplus cash|excess cash) to (shareholders|investors)\b
concepts.explainer:
When a company has more cash than it can invest at a good return, it returns it to shareholders in two ways.

A **dividend** is a cash payment per share. Cutting it is seen as a very negative signal, so companies raise it only if they think they can sustain it. A **buyback** (repurchase of the company's own shares) is more flexible: it can be stopped without drama. By reducing the number of shares, a buyback lifts **EPS** even when profit is unchanged.

Be careful: in theory, with no taxes and no mispricing, neither creates value, because both simply move cash from the company to its shareholders. A buyback creates value if the shares are bought below their intrinsic value, and destroys it if the company buys at too high a price or funds it with too much debt.

European and British banks often announce buybacks alongside their results, but only with the regulator's approval and if their capital (CET1) is above requirements.

What to watch: payout ratio, funding from cash or from debt, the price at which shares are repurchased.
concepts.interview:
A buyback or a dividend increase is an excellent starting point for discussing capital allocation: compare it with the alternatives (investing, acquiring, reducing debt). Show that you know a buyback increases EPS but not necessarily value.

EN: The buyback suggests management sees limited high-return investment opportunities and believes the shares are undervalued; it will be accretive to EPS, but it only creates value if the shares are bought below their intrinsic value.
watch: Is the buyback funded with free cash flow or with new debt?
What percentage of market capitalisation does it represent?
Is the dividend covered by earnings (payout ratio below 100%)?
Could the company invest at a higher return instead?

questions.stem: A company with net income of 100m and 50m shares outstanding buys back 10% of its shares. Assuming net income is unchanged, what is the new EPS?

steps: Initial EPS = 100 / 50 = 2.00.
After repurchasing 10%, 50 x 0.9 = 45 million shares remain.
In reality profit falls slightly, because the cash spent no longer earns interest, but the question rules this out.
explanation.shortcut: If the number of shares falls by a fraction x, EPS rises by 1 / (1 - x) - 1: with x = 10% that is about +11%.
explanation.trap: Answering 2.20 by adding 10%: it is the denominator that falls by 10%, so EPS rises by more.
explanation.rule: EPS = net income / number of shares: fewer shares with the same profit = higher EPS.

questions.stem: Why do companies usually prefer share buybacks to raising the regular dividend when their extra cash flow is uncertain?
options: Because buybacks are always taxed more heavily than dividends for shareholders
Because buybacks can be cut later without the negative signal of a dividend cut
Because buybacks increase net income directly, while dividends leave it unchanged
Because paying dividends reduces the number of shares outstanding over time

steps: The market sees the regular dividend as a commitment: a cut is read as a sign that management sees problems.
That is why companies raise the dividend only if they think they can sustain it over time (dividend smoothing).
A buyback, by contrast, can be reduced or stopped when cash falls, without a strong negative signal.
Uncertain or one-off extra cash is therefore better suited to a buyback or a special dividend.
explanation.shortcut: Stable cash = dividend; variable cash = buyback.
explanation.trap: Thinking that a buyback increases net income: it increases EPS only because it reduces the number of shares.
explanation.rule: Dividends are rigid, buybacks are flexible.

questions.stem: Under which condition does a share buyback create value for the shareholders who do not sell?
options: When the shares are repurchased below their intrinsic value
Whenever the buyback increases earnings per share
When it is funded with new debt, whatever the interest cost
When the share price is at an all-time high, signalling confidence

steps: A buyback is an exchange: the company hands over cash and retires shares.
If it pays less than intrinsic value, the shareholders who remain own a larger stake in a company worth more than what was spent: they gain.
If it pays more, it transfers value to the shareholders who sell.
The rise in EPS is almost automatic (it only requires the earnings yield to exceed the after-tax cost of cash), so it does not prove that value is being created.
explanation.shortcut: A buyback is an investment in the company's own shares: it creates value only if you buy them at a discount.
explanation.trap: Confusing EPS accretion with value creation: a buyback can raise EPS and still destroy value if the price is too high.
explanation.rule: A buyback creates value for the remaining shareholders only if the price paid is below intrinsic value.

pill.why: Buybacks and dividends usually signal confidence in cash generation; a buyback creates value only if shares are bought below intrinsic value without stretching the balance sheet.
pill.watch: The funding source (free cash flow or debt), size versus market cap and dividend cover.
pill.en: [Company] is returning [amount] via [buybacks/dividends], funded from [free cash flow/debt]; a buyback lifts EPS but only creates value if the shares are undervalued.

concepts.title: Restructurings and job cuts
match: \bjobs? (at risk|to go|are to go|will go|under threat)\b

\b(cut|cuts|cutting|axe|axes|axing|axed|shed|sheds|shedding|slash|slashes|slashing|slashed|eliminate|eliminates|eliminating|eliminated|scrap|scraps|scrapping|scrapped) (\d[\d,.]*k? |hundreds of |thousands of |hundreds |thousands |dozens |another |a further |further |an additional |more |about |around |up to |some |nearly |almost |a third of |a quarter of |\d+% of )*(its |their |the )?((?!(for|to|of|on|in|at|from|by|with|and|or|pay|tax|taxes|benefits?|support)\b)[\w-]+ )?(jobs|roles|positions|staff|workers|employees|workforce|headcount|posts)\b
concepts.explainer:
When a company announces **job cuts**, plant closures or a **restructuring** plan, it is trying to lower its cost base to protect its margins.

The accounting effect: in the short term there are one-off **restructuring costs** (severance payments, write-downs) that reduce reported profit; from the following years, the savings recur every year. That is why analysts look at **adjusted** profit, which excludes one-off items, and at the **payback**: how many years it takes for the savings to pay back the cost.

The market often rewards the announcement if the cuts are credible and demand is holding up, but punishes it if the cuts reveal a collapse in revenue. At macro level, waves of layoffs in a sector are a sign of a slowdown.

Who gains: shareholders, if margins improve. Who loses: employees and, sometimes, future growth, if research or the sales force are cut as well.

What to watch: expected annual savings, the one-off cost and why the cuts are being made right now.
concepts.interview:
A story about job cuts lets you show both financial and human sensitivity. Explain the effect on margins, separate one-off costs from recurring savings and ask yourself whether the problem is one of costs or of demand.

EN: The plan should save around [X] a year against a one-off cost of [Y], so the payback is under [Z] years; the real question is whether it fixes a cost problem or simply masks weakening demand.
watch: Expected annual savings relative to the one-off cost (payback)
Are the cuts a response to falling demand or to internal inefficiencies?
Is reported profit falling because of the plan's costs while adjusted profit improves?
Are other companies in the sector doing the same?

questions.stem: A company announces a restructuring with a one-off cost of 300m and expected annual savings of 150m from next year. Ignoring tax and the time value of money, what is the simple payback period?
options: 0.5 years
1 year
2 years
3 years

steps: Payback = one-off cost / annual savings.
After two years the savings have paid back the cost; from then on they improve margins every year.
explanation.shortcut: Divide the cost by the annual savings.
explanation.trap: Calculating 150 / 300 = 0.5 by inverting the ratio.
explanation.rule: Simple payback = initial investment / annual cash flow.

questions.stem: In the year a company books large restructuring charges, how are its reported and adjusted operating profit typically affected?
options: Reported profit falls, while adjusted profit excludes the one-off charges
Both fall by exactly the same amount
Adjusted profit falls, while reported profit is unchanged
Neither is affected, because restructuring charges go directly to equity

steps: Restructuring costs (severance payments, write-downs of plant) go through the income statement: reported profit falls.
Companies and analysts also present an adjusted profit that excludes one-off items, to show recurring profitability.
That is why, in the year of the plan, reported and adjusted profit diverge sharply.
explanation.shortcut: Reported includes everything; adjusted strips out exceptional items.
explanation.trap: Thinking the costs go directly to equity: they go through the income statement. And watch out for companies that have 'exceptional costs' every year.
explanation.rule: Always compare reported and adjusted profit, and ask yourself whether the one-off items recur.

questions.stem: Two companies announce identical job cuts. Company A has stable revenue and margins below its peers; Company B's revenue is falling sharply. How does the market usually read the two announcements?
options: Both should rise by the same amount, because the cost savings are identical in size
B should rise more, because it needs the savings more urgently than A does
Both should fall, because job cuts always signal financial distress to investors
A's cuts look like margin repair, B's like a response to falling demand

steps: The same cuts can tell different stories.
For A, with stable revenue and margins below its peers, the problem is efficiency: the savings drop through to margins (self-help).
For B, with falling revenue, the cuts are chasing declining demand: the savings risk being eaten up by falling volumes.
The market rewards A's story more and views B's with scepticism.
explanation.shortcut: Cuts + stable revenue = self-help; cuts + falling revenue = defence.
explanation.trap: Thinking that only the size of the savings matters: what matters is the revenue context.
explanation.rule: Always read cuts together with revenue: a cost problem or a demand problem?

pill.why: Restructurings usually hit reported profit with one-off costs before savings arrive; markets tend to reward credible cuts but punish those that reveal falling demand.
pill.watch: Annual savings versus one-off costs, the payback period, and whether peers are cutting too.
pill.en: [Company] expects [amount] of annual savings for a one-off cost of [amount], a [X]-year payback; the question is whether it is fixing inefficiency or reacting to weaker demand.

concepts.title: Corporate distress and insolvencies
match: \b(enters?|entered|entering|faces?|facing|faced|heads? for|heading for|headed for|edges? (closer )?(to|towards)|edging (closer )?(to|towards)|brink of|verge of|close to|nears?|nearing|avoids?|avoided|avoiding|staves? off|staved off|calls? in|called in) (special )?administration\b(?! (officials?|pressure|policy|policies|criticism|scrutiny|crackdown|demands?|orders?|probe|says|said|plans?|figures?|staff)\b)
exclude: \b(mortgages?|mortgage holders|credit cards?|student loans?|car loans?|auto loans?|homeowners|first-time buyers)\b
concepts.explainer:
A company enters **distress** when it can no longer pay interest or refinance maturing debt. The options are a **debt restructuring** negotiated with creditors or a formal procedure, such as **Chapter 11** in the US (the company keeps operating while it restructures) or **administration** in the UK.

The central rule is the **priority of claims** (waterfall): first secured creditors, then senior unsecured creditors, then subordinated creditors and lastly shareholders. Shareholders are usually wiped out, while creditors often convert their debt into shares (debt-for-equity swap) and become the new owners.

Distress shows up first in prices: bonds trade well below par (for example 40 per 100 of face value), ratings fall towards CCC and suppliers ask to be paid in advance.

What to watch: leverage, debt maturities, available liquidity, bond prices and the expected recovery for each class of creditor.
concepts.interview:
A story about an insolvency lets you talk about capital structure and creditor priority, core topics in restructuring and leveraged finance. Explain why the company ended up there (too much leverage, a collapse in demand, higher interest rates) and who recovers what.

EN: The company's problem looks more like a balance-sheet issue than an operating one: the business is still viable but cannot refinance its debt at current rates, so I would expect creditors to take control through a debt-for-equity swap and shareholders to be largely wiped out.
watch: A liquidity problem (maturities) or a solvency problem (unsustainable business)?
At what price do the bonds trade relative to 100?
Who is secured and who is not in the capital structure?
Are there buyers for the assets or a rescue plan?

questions.stem: In a corporate bankruptcy, which group is typically paid last?
options: Secured lenders
Senior unsecured bondholders
Subordinated bondholders
Ordinary shareholders

steps: The waterfall pays out in order of priority: secured, senior unsecured, subordinated, equity.
Shareholders have a residual claim: they receive something only if all creditors are repaid in full.
In a bankruptcy the value is usually not enough, and shareholders are wiped out.
explanation.shortcut: Equity is always at the back of the queue.
explanation.trap: Confusing subordinated creditors with shareholders: subordinated bonds are still debt and rank ahead of equity.
explanation.rule: Priority: secured, then senior unsecured, then subordinated, and finally equity.

questions.stem: A distressed company is worth an enterprise value of 600m in restructuring. It has 400m of secured debt and 500m of unsecured bonds. Assuming strict priority, what recovery do the unsecured bondholders receive?

steps: The value available is 600.
Secured creditors are paid first: 400 out of 400, repaid in full.
That leaves 600 - 400 = 200 for the unsecured creditors, whose claims total 500: recovery = 200 / 500 = 40%.
Nothing is left for shareholders.
explanation.shortcut: Subtract the higher-priority claims, then divide what remains by the claims of the class.
explanation.trap: Calculating 600 / 900 = 67% by sharing the value pro rata among all creditors: this ignores the priority of the secured creditors.
explanation.rule: Recovery for a class = value remaining after the higher-ranking classes / claims of the class (maximum 100%).

questions.stem: Over a few months, a company's bonds fall from 95 to 45 (per 100 of face value) and its shares lose 90% of their value, while government bond yields are broadly unchanged. What is the market most likely pricing?
options: A general rise in risk-free interest rates that has hit all bonds in the market
An imminent takeover of the company at a premium to the current share price
A high risk of default, with partial recovery for bonds and little for shares
A temporary liquidity problem in the bond market that will reverse within weeks

steps: A healthy bond trades close to 100. At 45 the market considers full repayment unlikely.

Bond price ≈ probability of repayment x 100 + probability of default x recovery. If default is almost certain, the price approaches the expected recovery; if some chance of full repayment remains, the implied recovery is even lower than 45.
A share that loses 90% indicates that shareholders expect to be left with little or nothing: in a restructuring they are paid last.
Government bond yields have not moved, so the collapse is specific to the company: it is credit risk, not interest rate risk.
explanation.shortcut: A single company's bonds well below par and its shares plunging, with government bonds unchanged: the market is pricing in default and partial recovery.
explanation.trap: Attributing the fall to interest rates: a rise in rates would hit all bonds and would not explain the 90% collapse in the shares. Remember, though, that low-coupon, very long-dated bonds can fall a lot on rates alone: that is why you always compare with government bonds.
explanation.rule: In distress the bond price tends towards the expected recovery and equity tends towards zero.

pill.why: When a company cannot refinance, value is usually split by creditor priority: secured lenders tend to recover most, shareholders are often wiped out and creditors may take control.
pill.watch: Whether it is a liquidity or solvency problem, bond prices versus par, and expected recoveries.
pill.en: [Company]'s bonds trade at [X] cents on the [dollar/euro], pricing a restructuring in which [secured lenders/bondholders] would likely take control and shareholders would be largely wiped out.

concepts.title: Debt issuance and credit ratings
match: \b(sells?|sold|selling|issues|issued|issuing|taps?|tapped|tapping|launch(?:es|ed|ing)?|prices|priced|pricing|takes orders for|seeks?)( (\$|£|€|us\$)\s?\d[\d.,]*\s?(bn|billion|m|mn|million))?( of| worth of| in)?( (new|fresh|green|dollar|euro|sterling|senior|hybrid|convertible|perpetual|subordinated|long-dated|\d+-year))* (bonds?|debt|notes|eurobonds?)\b
exclude: \b(mortgages?|remortgag\w*|homeowners|homebuyers|student loans?|credit cards?|household debt|consumer credit|personal loans?|buy now,? pay later)\b
concepts.explainer:
Companies fund themselves with bank loans or by issuing **bonds**. The cost of debt is roughly: the risk-free rate (the yield on government bonds) + the **credit spread**, the premium for the risk of that specific company.

The **rating agencies** (S&P, Moody's, Fitch) assess the ability to repay. The key threshold separates **investment grade** (BBB- / Baa3 and above) from **high yield** or junk (below). Many institutional investors can hold only investment grade: a **downgrade** below that threshold (fallen angel) triggers forced selling and a jump in the spread.

A bond's price and yield move in opposite directions: if perceived risk rises, the price falls and the yield rises, and new issues cost more.

The metrics that agencies and banks look at are **leverage** (net debt / EBITDA) and **interest cover** (EBITDA / interest). A debt-financed acquisition can push the rating down.

What to watch: the level of spreads, demand in new issues (how many times the book is covered), maturities to be refinanced and the rating outlook.
concepts.interview:
A news story on a bond issue or a downgrade lets you connect corporate finance and markets. Explain what changes for the company's cost of capital and for those who hold its bonds.

EN: The downgrade to [rating] matters because it takes the company closer to high yield, which would widen its spreads and raise its refinancing costs, so I would expect management to prioritise deleveraging over buybacks.
watch: Is the rating close to the threshold between investment grade and high yield?
Is leverage (net debt / EBITDA) rising or falling?
Is the issue heavily oversubscribed? At what spread over government bonds?
How much debt matures in the next 2-3 years?

questions.stem: A rating agency downgrades a company's credit rating. Other things equal, what happens to the price and the yield of the company's existing fixed-rate bonds?
options: The price falls and the yield rises
The price rises and the yield falls
The price and the yield both rise
Neither changes, because the coupon is fixed

steps: A downgrade means higher credit risk: investors demand a wider spread.
The coupon on the existing bond is fixed, so the only way to offer a higher yield is a lower price.
Price down, yield up: this is the inverse relationship between price and yield.
explanation.shortcut: Risk up = spread up = price down.
explanation.trap: Thinking the fixed coupon locks everything in place: the coupon does not change, but the price adjusts and with it the yield to maturity.
explanation.rule: A bond's price and yield always move in opposite directions.

questions.stem: A company's rating is cut from BBB- to BB+. Why can this one-notch move raise its borrowing costs much more than a cut from A to A-?
options: Because bonds rated BB+ can no longer be traded on public exchanges
Because the rating agency directly resets the coupon on all of the company's existing bonds
Because it crosses into high yield, forcing sales by investors restricted to investment grade
Because a move from A to A- is not counted as a downgrade under the agencies' rules

steps: BBB- is the last investment-grade notch; BB+ is the first high-yield (junk) notch.
Many funds and insurers, because of their mandates or capital rules, can hold only investment grade or very little high yield.
The move forces selling, the investor base shrinks and the spread jumps (the fallen-angel effect).
From A to A-, by contrast, the company stays well within investment grade: the spread widens only slightly.
explanation.shortcut: Crossing the BBB- / BB+ line is the most expensive downgrade.
explanation.trap: Thinking every rating notch is worth the same: the investment-grade threshold creates a jump.
explanation.rule: The cliff effect between investment grade and high yield makes the move from BBB- to BB+ the most expensive.

questions.stem: A company with EBITDA of 200m and net debt of 400m issues 600m of new bonds to buy a business with EBITDA of 50m on a cash-free, debt-free basis, paying entirely with the proceeds. What happens to its net leverage (net debt / EBITDA)?
options: It rises from 2.0x to 5.0x
It rises from 2.0x to 4.0x
It stays at 2.0x
It falls from 2.0x to 1.6x

steps: Starting leverage = 400 / 200 = 2.0x.
After the deal: net debt 400 + 600 = 1000; EBITDA 200 + 50 = 250.
New leverage = 1000 / 250 = 4.0x: it doubles, and the rating may be at risk.
The price paid is 12x the target's EBITDA (600 / 50), well above the starting leverage: that is why leverage rises.
explanation.shortcut: Add the debt, add the EBITDA, then divide: buying at a high multiple with debt pushes leverage up.
explanation.trap: Forgetting the target's EBITDA (5.0x) or forgetting the new debt (1.6x).
explanation.rule: Net leverage = net debt / EBITDA, both pro forma after the deal.

pill.why: Ratings and spreads usually set how much companies pay to borrow, and a downgrade below investment grade can trigger forced selling and a jump in funding costs.
pill.watch: Distance from the investment-grade threshold, leverage trend, order book coverage and upcoming maturities.
pill.en: [Company]'s [bond issue/rating action] matters because, at [rating] with leverage of [X]x EBITDA, its position versus the investment-grade line decides who can hold the debt and at what spread.

concepts.title: Banks: margins, capital and profits
concepts.explainer:
A commercial bank earns mainly from **net interest income** (NII): the difference between what it earns on loans and what it pays on deposits. The **net interest margin** (NIM) is this income as a percentage of interest-earning assets.

When rates rise, loans usually reprice faster than deposits and the NIM widens: that is why European banks' profits rose sharply after 2022. When rates fall, the margin is squeezed. But high rates also increase **non-performing loans** and loan-loss provisions.

Banks must meet **capital requirements** (Basel III): the **CET1 ratio** (highest-quality capital / risk-weighted assets, RWA) must stay above a minimum. More capital means more safety but a lower return on capital (RoTE); excess capital is returned through dividends and buybacks, if the regulator allows it.

What to watch: NII and NIM, cost of risk, CET1 ratio, RoTE and price relative to tangible book value (P/TBV).
concepts.interview:
Banks are the most natural topic for anyone applying to a bank: it links results to interest rates and the credit cycle. Show that you know high rates help margins but can worsen credit quality.

EN: For banks the key driver is net interest income: if rates [fall/stay high], I would expect margins to [narrow/hold up], so I would focus on fee income, cost control and whether loan-loss provisions start to rise.
watch: Is net interest income rising or falling with rates?
Are loan-loss provisions increasing?
CET1 ratio versus the requirement: is there excess capital to distribute?
Does RoTE exceed the cost of capital required by investors?

questions.stem: When interest rates rise, why do the profits of a traditional retail bank usually increase, at least at first?
options: Because higher rates immediately reduce loan defaults across the bank's loan book
Because asset yields reprice faster than deposit rates, widening the net interest margin
Because the bank's capital requirements fall when rates rise, freeing up capital to lend
Because deposit rates usually rise by more than loan rates, attracting new savers

steps: Net interest income depends on the difference between the rate on loans and the rate on deposits.
When rates rise, floating-rate loans, new loans and invested cash reprice quickly, while banks raise deposit rates slowly (low deposit beta).
The margin widens and profits rise. Over time, competition for deposits and credit losses erode part of the gain; a bank full of long-dated fixed-rate loans or securities benefits much less.
explanation.shortcut: Rates up: assets reprice before liabilities, so a wider NIM.
explanation.trap: Thinking high rates reduce defaults: they usually increase them, because borrowers face higher repayments.
explanation.rule: The NIM widens when rates rise and the deposit beta is low.

questions.stem: A bank has CET1 capital of 15bn and risk-weighted assets of 100bn. Its CET1 requirement is 11%. How much CET1 capital does it hold above the requirement?
options: 0.6bn
11bn
4bn

steps: CET1 ratio = CET1 / RWA = 15 / 100 = 15%.
Required capital = 11% x 100 = 11bn.
Excess = 15 - 11 = 4bn, i.e. 4 percentage points of RWA: this is the buffer the bank can use to grow or to distribute, while keeping a safety margin.
explanation.shortcut: Excess in billions = (CET1 ratio - requirement) x RWA = 4% x 100.
explanation.trap: Applying the percentage to capital instead of RWA (11% x 15 = 1.65): the requirement is calculated on risk-weighted assets.
explanation.rule: CET1 ratio = CET1 / RWA; the requirement applies to RWA.

questions.stem: A bank earns a return on tangible equity (RoTE) of 8%, while its cost of equity is 11%. Assuming no growth, how is it most likely to trade relative to its tangible book value?
options: Above tangible book value, because its RoTE is positive
At exactly tangible book value, because book value is audited
Below tangible book value, roughly 0.7x
It cannot be related to tangible book value

steps: What a bank is worth relative to its book value depends on how much its capital earns compared with what investors require.
With no growth: P/TBV = RoTE / cost of capital = 8% / 11% = about 0.73.
If RoTE is below the cost of capital, each euro of capital earns less than required: the market prices the bank below book value.
Many European banks traded below tangible book value for years for precisely this reason.
explanation.shortcut: RoTE above the cost of capital: above book; below it: below book.
explanation.trap: Thinking a positive RoTE is enough to trade above book: it must exceed the cost of capital.
explanation.rule: P/TBV is roughly equal to RoTE / cost of capital (with no growth).

pill.why: Bank profits usually track interest rates through net interest margin, while loan losses and capital ratios decide how much can be returned to shareholders.
pill.watch: The net interest income trend, cost of risk, CET1 versus requirements and RoTE.
pill.en: [Bank]'s net interest income [rose/fell] [X%] with CET1 at [X%]; the key questions are whether rates keep supporting margins and whether excess capital funds [buybacks/dividends].

concepts.title: AI, technology and semiconductors
concepts.explainer:
The **artificial intelligence** investment cycle runs through three links: those who make the **chips** (GPUs, memory, foundries), those who build the **data centres** (the big cloud groups, known as hyperscalers, which spend enormous sums on **capex**) and those who use AI in their own products. One group's capex is another group's revenue: when the big cloud players raise their spending plans, the suppliers of chips, power and networking go up.

**Semiconductors** have historically been a **cyclical** sector: shortages and high prices encourage building capacity, then oversupply arrives and prices collapse. AI demand has made the cycle stronger and more concentrated.
